A file with no `import` and no `export` is valid both as a script and as a module, and the two run differently: a module is in strict mode, its top-level `this` is `undefined`, and its top-level declarations are not global. A tool that has to guess from the content can guess wrong.

One `import` or `export` statement settles it. `import()`, `import.meta`, top-level `await` and `require()` do not count.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
function greet(name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}`);
}

greet("Ada");
```

{/* bad */}
```js
const { greet } = await import("./greet.js");

greet("Ada");
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
export function greet(name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}`);
}
```

If the file has nothing to export, an empty export marks it as a module:

{/* good */}
```js
function greet(name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}`);
}

greet("Ada");

export {};
```

A `.cjs` file is never a module, so it is not checked:

{/* good {"filename": "greet.cjs"} */}
```js greet.cjs
console.log("Hello, Ada");
```

## When not to use it

If every tool you use decides by the file extension or by `"type"` in `package.json`, the content of the file does not matter and this rule is noise.
